Lessons.Title: Graphing the Standard Form (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: explore how changing linear coefficient b in ax²+bx+c changes the graph's symmetry axis and vertex when a and c remain fixed. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of optional Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U06:L13 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/6/13/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/6/13/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The publisher explicitly makes this optional and asks learners to notice graphs; it does not require general mastery of graph transformations at this point.

Original two functions f(x)=x²−6x and g(x)=x²+2x share a=1,c=0, so both pass origin(0,0) and open upward. Factoring yields f=x(x−6) with zeros0,6 and axis x3; g=x(x+2) with zeros0,−2 and axis x−1. Their vertices are f(3)=−9 and g(−1)=−1. Changing b affects both horizontal and vertical positions of the vertices.

For general a≠0, axis x=−b/(2a), derived by completing square. Keeping a1,c0, changing b alone changes the x-coordinate of the vertex but does not change y-intercept(0,0). This shows why a description such as 'adding bx just shifts left' may omit a vertical change.

Student task: graph three variations with a1,c0 and b=−6,0,+2; use tables to locate symmetrical pairs and explain how axis moves. If using actual graphing technology, record that separately; a static plot description is not evidence of live slider interaction. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for correct tables, axes/vertices, parameter isolation and explanatory comparisons.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear coefficient b
KeyConcepts.Definition: For ax²+bx+c, b participates in determining symmetry axis and vertex.
KeyConcepts.Example: b−6 with a1 gives axis x3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intercept invariant when c fixed
KeyConcepts.Definition: At x0, ax²+bx+c=c regardless of b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factoring reveals symmetry
KeyConcepts.Definition: When zeros are visible, vertex x-coordinate is root midpoint.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare b variations
WorkedExamples.Question: What stays the same if b changes but a=1,c=0?
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate explicit first-party quadratic coefficients and check graph features via algebra.
Steps: All functions have quadratic coefficient+1 and open upward.
Vertex height also varies because substituting the axis input changes output.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Same opening and y-intercept; different vertices.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming changing b shifts graph only horizontally
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Vertex height also changes when c is fixed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mistaking optional exploratory source lesson for full vertex-algebra mastery
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source asks for observation and reasoning.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use tables and transparent model comparisons.

SummaryPoints: Linear coefficient b affects the symmetry axis and vertex.
Holding c constant keeps the y-intercept unchanged.
Factoring gives f and g roots and vertex positions.
